analysis.one_liner: Makes large Wall Street firms pay in advance into a federal fund to cover the cost of their own future failures instead of taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 111th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a "Systemic Resolution Fund" at the FDIC — a reserve of money supplied by fees on large financial companies that pose a risk to the whole system. If one of those giants failed, the fund would cover the cost of shutting it down and stabilizing the system, so taxpayers would not be asked to foot the bill the way they were during the 2008 bailouts. Firms judged not to pose a systemic risk, like small community banks, would be exempt, and the fund could not exceed 1 percent of the size of the U.S. economy. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the bill passes: the cost of unwinding a failed giant financial firm would be prepaid by the industry itself through assessments, rather than charged to taxpayers after a crisis, as happened with the 2008 bailouts. Small banks benefit too, since the FDIC is barred from assessing firms it determines do not pose a systemic risk. The FDIC gains a new dedicated fund and assessment authority to do its job as receiver for failing large firms.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Systemic Resolution Fund run by the FDIC to cover the costs of winding down a failing large financial company, so taxpayers do not absorb those costs directly [S2][S3].

Requires the FDIC to charge financial companies ongoing assessments to maintain the fund, and to replenish it within about eight years after any drawdown, so the industry pays for its own failures in advance rather than after the fact [S3].

Prohibits charging any financial company the FDIC determines does not pose a systemic risk, which would spare small banks and community lenders from paying into a fund aimed at the largest firms [S3].

Caps the fund at 1 percent of U.S. GDP and requires annual reallocation of assessments among systemically risky firms based on the risk they pose, including their off-balance-sheet activities, so the firms whose behavior creates the danger pay proportionally more [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large financial companies that pose systemic risk pay assessments to build and replenish the fund, sized by their risk profile, including off-balance-sheet activities; those costs could partly be passed to customers through fees. The Treasury also initially capitalizes the fund with appropriated money, which the assessments later repay.

drawbacks.text: Assessments on banks are ultimately paid by someone: banks could pass some of the cost to customers through higher fees or lower interest on deposits, though the bill lets regulators spread assessments based on risk and consider assessments firms already pay to deposit insurance, securities, and state insurance funds [S3].

A pre-funded pool of up to 1 percent of GDP creates a standing pot of money that could invite pressure to use it to keep failing firms alive; the bill tries to guard against this by barring the fund from being used to convert or maintain an insolvent company except when needed for systemic stabilization [S3].

The bill relies on the FDIC to define and predict which firms pose systemic risk and to price assessments correctly; misjudging that could leave the fund either too small in a crisis or a needless burden in calm times [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but hard to measure: a pre-funded resolution reserve would make future failures of giant financial firms cheaper for taxpayers and less disruptive, and the fund is capped at 1 percent of GDP with small firms exempt. The cost is that the companies paying the assessments would likely pass some of them to customers, and a large pre-funded pool could tempt Congress or regulators to use it for rescues rather than wind-downs — which the bill tries to prevent by barring use of the fund to prop up insolvent firms [S2][S3]. A fair reading is that the bill was a reasonable insurance mechanism with modest, arguable costs, and it never got enough support even to be tested. Its core idea moved into the broader 2010 financial reform debate through other vehicles rather than this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day; the committee never took it up, no cosponsors joined, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions were introduction and referral: on March 1, 2010, Senator Menendez introduced it, it was read twice, and it was referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5][S1].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list is empty [S4].
The committee never reported the bill, no markup or hearing is recorded in the action history, and no floor vote ever occurred [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired with it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial companies came out ahead: they never had to pay assessments into a pre-funded resolution reserve. Ordinary taxpayers remained the ultimate backstop for future failures of big financial firms.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 1, 2010, establishing an FDIC-administered Systemic Resolution Fund financed by assessments on systemically risky financial companies [S1][S2][S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 1, 2010 and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, leaving its partisan shape untested [S4][S5].

industries.note: These firms would have paid ongoing assessments to build and replenish a resolution fund capped at 1 percent of GDP, sized by the risk they pose, including off-balance-sheet activities. The bill died, so they never paid; the bill's death also meant they avoided an industry-funded backstop for their own failures.

industries.industry: Small banks and non-systemic financial firms
industries.note: The bill bars the FDIC from assessing any financial company it determines does not pose systemic risk, sparing smaller institutions the cost of a fund aimed at the giants. They kept that exemption by the bill not passing only because they were never charged in the first place.

Taxpayers have repeatedly been the backstop when major financial firms fail, as in the 2008 bailouts. A pre-funded industry reserve would have put the first line of defense on the firms themselves. The bill's failure left the taxpayer as the ultimate backstop, though separate 2010 financial reform legislation took up the wind-down question in other ways.
